q: Why can the G1's whole skeleton be stored as one integer array, body_parentid?
choices: Every body has exactly one parent, so one integer per body suffices
Every body has exactly one child, so the array lists the children
Body ids are given in depth order, so the ids encode the tree
Only the five chains are stored, one integer per chain
why: That is the definition of a tree. Ancestors, depth and children all follow by repeating π(b) = parent of b.

q: In body_parentid, π(0) = 0. What does that mean?
choices: Body 0 is the world, and it is its own parent
Body 0 is the pelvis, which has no parent
Body 0 is a leaf, with no children of its own
The tree has not been compiled from the MJCF yet
why: The world is body 0 and the root of the tree. Following parents from any body ends at 0; the pelvis hangs off it through the free joint.

q: How many bodies and leaves does the G1 tree have?
choices: 31 bodies (one is the world); 4 leaves: feet and hands
30 bodies, 5 leaves: two feet, two hands and the head
31 bodies and 2 leaves: only the two feet
36 bodies, one per qpos slot, with 4 leaves
why: nbody = 31 including the world. The four leaves are the ankle-roll links and wrist-yaw links; the head is welded to the torso, not a body with its own branch.

q: A toy robot has body_parentid = [0, 0, 1, 2, 1, 4]. Which bodies are leaves?
choices: Bodies 3 and 5
Bodies 0 and 1
Bodies 2 and 4
Body 5 only
why: A leaf is a body nobody names as parent. The parents listed are 0, 1, 2, 1, 4, so 3 and 5 never appear. Body 1 has two children (2 and 4).

q: Same toy tree, body_parentid = [0, 0, 1, 2, 1, 4], one hinge per body 1..5. Which bodies' joints can move body 5?
choices: Bodies 1, 4 and 5
Bodies 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5
Bodies 4 and 5 only
Bodies 2 and 3
why: Ancestors of 5: π(5) = 4, π(4) = 1, π(1) = 0. A joint moves body k iff its body is k or an ancestor of k, so 1, 4, 5. Bodies 2 and 3 are on another branch.

q: Which sum gives the G1's 29 hinges (= nu)?
choices: 6 + 6 + 3 + 7 + 7: two legs, waist, two arms
7 + 7 + 3 + 6 + 6: two legs, waist, two arms
6 + 6 + 3 + 7 + 7 + 1: plus one head joint
6 + 6 + 5 + 6 + 6: legs, waist, arms
why: Legs have 6 each, the waist 3, arms 7 each: 29 = nu. There is no head, neck or hand joint.

q: Where does the left arm live in qpos and qvel?
why: Chain table: left leg 7..12/6..11, right leg 13..18/12..17, waist 19..21/18..20, left arm 22..28/21..27, right arm 29..35/28..34. qvel is always one lower.

q: Where do the G1's arms attach to the tree?
choices: To the torso, three waist joints above the pelvis
To the pelvis, alongside the two legs
To the waist-yaw link, one joint above the pelvis
To the head, which hangs off the torso
why: The legs hang off the pelvis; the arms hang off the torso, three waist joints up. So the waist moves both arms and neither leg.

q: How is each chain laid out in qpos?
choices: Contiguous, in root-to-tip order
Contiguous, but in tip-to-root order
Interleaved left and right, joint by joint
Scattered in id order, with gaps between chains
why: Each chain occupies one slice root to tip, and together they cover slots 7..35. That is why set_pose can take a whole chain as a list.

q: Which Python slice of data.qpos is the right arm?
why: Right arm = slots 29..35, and a slice's end is exclusive, so 29:36. 28:35 is its qvel range; 22:29 is the left arm.

q: When can joint j move landmark k? (β(j) = the body joint j turns, A(k) = ancestors of k.)
choices: When β(j) = k or β(j) ∈ A(k)
When k ∈ A(β(j))
When β(j) and k are in the same chain
When j's qpos index is below k's body id
why: A joint turns its own body and everything downstream. k ∈ A(β(j)) is the reverse: k upstream of the joint, which it can never move.

q: Practice Q8, first half: which of the five landmarks (two hands, two feet, torso IMU) does right_hip_yaw move?
choices: Only the right foot
Both feet, through the pelvis
The right foot and the torso IMU
The right foot and the right hand
why: The right leg hangs off the pelvis and is its own branch; the only landmark downstream of right_hip_yaw is the right foot. A leg joint moves one foot and nothing else.

q: Practice Q8, second half: which landmarks does waist_roll move?
choices: Both hands and the torso IMU, neither foot
Both feet and the torso IMU, neither hand
Every landmark, since the waist is central
Only the torso IMU, which rides on torso_link
why: The torso and both arms are downstream of the waist; the legs hang off the pelvis below it. A waist joint moves both hands and neither foot.

q: Of the 29 hinges, which can move the torso IMU site?
choices: Only the three waist joints
The waist joints and both shoulder pitches
All 29, since everything hangs off the pelvis
Only waist_pitch
why: The IMU is on torso_link, whose ancestors (besides the pelvis) are the three waist links. Leg and arm joints are on other branches or downstream.

q: Nudging one left-leg joint by 0.1 rad from stand, how far does the left foot move?
choices: Hip pitch 65 mm, knee 32 mm, ankle pitch 2 mm
Hip pitch 2 mm, knee 32 mm, ankle pitch 65 mm
Hip pitch 32 mm, knee 65 mm, ankle pitch 2 mm
Hip pitch 65 mm, knee 65 mm, ankle pitch 65 mm
why: Within a limb the effect falls from root to tip. "The root of a chain is always the loud one; an ankle is for trimming."

q: Why does a joint's effect on its landmark fall from root to tip?
choices: A joint carries everything below it, so the root has the longest lever
Root joints have stronger motors, so they move further per radian
Tip joints have narrower range limits than the root joints
The nudge is scaled down at each joint further down the chain
why: Distance moved ≈ lever × angle, and the hip is farthest from the foot. Motor strength does not enter kinematics at all.

q: A 0.1 rad nudge of the knee moves the foot 32 mm. Roughly how long is the knee's lever arm?
choices: About 0.32 m
About 3.2 m
About 0.032 m
About 0.0032 m
why: Arc ≈ r·θ, so r ≈ 0.032 m / 0.1 rad = 0.32 m, matching week 2's knee column of 0.32 m/rad.

q: Which three joints move their landmark by exactly zero?
choices: Ankle roll, wrist roll, wrist yaw
Ankle pitch, wrist pitch, elbow
Hip yaw, waist yaw, wrist yaw
Ankle roll, hip roll, shoulder roll
why: Each landmark sits on that joint's own axis, and spinning a point about a line through itself does not move it.

q: ankle_roll moves the foot landmark by exactly 0 mm. What does it still do?
choices: It rotates the foot: orientation changes, position does not
Nothing at all: it is a modelling artefact of the MJCF
It moves the other foot instead, through the pelvis
It moves the foot only once gravity is switched on
why: Position is only half a pose. The three on-axis joints rotate their landmark (28.6° per 0.5 rad), which is why IK solving both position and orientation needs them.

q: Practice Q7: the left knee is at qpos[10]. Which qvel index holds its velocity?
choices: qvel[9]
qvel[10]
qvel[11]
qvel[4]
why: For every one of the 29 hinges, qpos index − qvel index = 1, so 10 − 1 = 9. Using 10 would read the left ankle pitch's velocity.

q: Where is the right knee in qpos and in qvel?
choices: qpos[16], qvel[15]
qpos[15], qvel[16]
qpos[16], qvel[16]
qpos[10], qvel[9]
why: Right leg = qpos 13..18 in order hip pitch, hip roll, hip yaw, knee, ankle pitch, ankle roll, so the knee is 16, and qvel one lower, 15. qpos 10 is the left knee.

q: The left arm is qpos 22..28: shoulder pitch, roll, yaw, elbow, wrist roll, pitch, yaw. Where is the left elbow?
choices: qpos[25], qvel[24]
qpos[24], qvel[25]
qpos[25], qvel[25]
qpos[26], qvel[25]
why: Elbow is the 4th joint: 22 + 3 = 25 in qpos; qvel is always one lower, 24.

q: Code runs data.qpos[dof_index('left_knee')] = 1.0. What actually happens?
choices: The left hip yaw (qpos[9]) is set, silently
The left knee is set; both indices work on qpos
The left ankle pitch (qpos[11]) is set, silently
MuJoCo raises an IndexError
why: dof_index gives 9, a valid qpos slot that belongs to the neighbouring joint, left hip yaw. Nothing raises, nothing warns.

q: qvel index 6 is left_hip_pitch's velocity. What does qpos[6] hold?
choices: The z component of the pelvis quaternion
The left hip pitch angle, same slot as qvel
The pelvis's height z above the floor
The left hip roll angle
why: qpos 0..2 are pelvis position and 3..6 its quaternion (w, x, y, z), so qpos[6] is the quaternion's z. Hip pitch's angle is qpos[7].

q: Why is qpos index − qvel index exactly 1 for every G1 hinge?
choices: Only the free joint, listed first, has nq − nv = 1; hinges add 0
Each hinge stores its angle plus one extra sign slot in qpos
qvel starts at index 1, because qvel[0] holds the time
The quaternion and the position each add one extra slot
why: i_q(j) − i_v(j) = Σ_{k<j} (n_q(k) − n_v(k)). Hinges cost 1/1; the free joint costs 7/6 and comes first in the file.

q: A robot's MJCF lists a free joint, then a ball joint, then hinges. For a hinge after both, what is its qpos index − qvel index?
why: Free: 7 − 6 = 1. Ball: 4 − 3 = 1. Each hinge: 0. The running total is 2.

q: The G1's sizes: nq, nv and nu?
choices: nq 36, nv 35, nu 29
nq 35, nv 36, nu 29
nq 36, nv 35, nu 30
nq 36, nv 36, nu 29
why: nq = 7 + 29, nv = 6 + 29, nu = 29 actuators, one per hinge. The free joint is not actuated (the robot is underactuated).

q: Why is njnt = 30 on the G1?
choices: 1 free joint + 29 hinges
29 hinges + 1 weld for the head
30 hinges, one of them unactuated
5 chains × 6 joints each
why: The floating base is a joint too (type free). The head is welded, which is not a joint.

q: q̇ = ½ q ⊗ (0, ω). What does this rule guarantee?
choices: ‖q‖ stays 1; the rate is set by the 3 numbers of ω
q turns at twice the angular speed ω, by the ½
The scalar part w never changes during the motion
qpos and qvel end up the same length after integrating
why: d/dt ‖q‖² = 2 q·q̇ = 0, so it stays unit. One constraint on four numbers leaves three freedoms: why rotation costs 4 in qpos but 3 in qvel.

q: mj_integratePos spins the base at 0.5 rad/s about z for 1 s. What base quaternion results?
why: The turn is 0.5 rad, and a quaternion holds half the angle: (cos 0.25, 0, 0, sin 0.25). Just adding qvel·dt to qpos would give the wrong shape.

q: The base spins at π/2 rad/s about z for 1 s. What is the resulting base quaternion (w, x, y, z)?
why: Angle = 90°; half angle 45°: (cos 45°, 0, 0, sin 45°). (0, 0, 0, 1) is the full-angle slip (a 180° turn); (1, 0, 0, 1.571) is qpos += qvel·dt.

q: With M = diag(1, −1, 1), what is the mirror image of a rotation R?
choices: M R M
M R
Rᵀ, the inverse
−R, every entry negated
why: Reflect the point to the other side, turn it there, reflect back: p′ = M R M p. M R alone has det −1, not a rotation.

q: Under the left↔right mirror, what happens to the three kinds of joint angle?
choices: Roll and yaw negate; pitch keeps its sign
Pitch negates; roll and yaw keep their signs
All three negate
Only yaw negates
why: Entry (i, k) of M R M flips iff exactly one of i, k is y. Rx and Rz have their ±s in a y row/column, so they flip; Ry's ±s sit at (x, z) and (z, x).

q: What is M Rz(30°) M, with M = diag(1, −1, 1)?
why: The −s and +s of Rz sit at (x, y) and (y, x), each touching the y index once, so both flip: Rz(−30°). Yaw negates under the mirror.

q: Left leg pose: hip_pitch −0.3, hip_roll +0.1, hip_yaw +0.05. What is the mirrored right-leg pose?
choices: hip_pitch −0.3, hip_roll −0.1, hip_yaw −0.05
hip_pitch +0.3, hip_roll −0.1, hip_yaw −0.05
hip_pitch +0.3, hip_roll +0.1, hip_yaw +0.05
hip_pitch −0.3, hip_roll −0.1, hip_yaw +0.05
why: Negate roll and yaw, keep pitch. soc4180.mirror flips any joint whose name contains roll or yaw.

q: The stand keyframe has left arm [0.2, 0.2, 0, 1.28, …] and right arm [0.2, −0.2, 0, 1.28, …]. Which joint changed sign?
choices: Shoulder roll
Shoulder pitch
Elbow
Shoulder yaw
why: Arm order is shoulder pitch, roll, yaw, elbow, … The 2nd entry, shoulder roll, flips; pitch (0.2) and elbow (1.28) keep. The model's own keyframe proves the rule.

q: Why does the mirror rule work on joint angles alone, using only each joint's name?
choices: Every right joint turns about the same axis as its left twin
Every right joint's axis is the negative of its left twin's
MuJoCo stores the right side's angles already mirrored
The G1 model is symmetric to machine precision
why: M R M is a statement about rotations; it becomes 'negate roll and yaw angles' only because both sides share axes. With reversed axes the signs would come out the other way.

q: Which statement about mj_forward is right?
choices: qpos in, x quantities and subtree CoM out; no time passes
It advances time by 2 ms using ctrl, qvel and contacts
It reads ctrl and drives each joint's servo toward it
It integrates qvel into qpos, then computes xpos
why: Kinematics: nothing falls, ctrl is ignored. mj_step is dynamics: uses ctrl, qvel, contacts, advances 2 ms, and the robot can fall.

q: How much time does one G1 mj_step advance?
choices: 2 ms
0 ms
10 ms
1 ms
why: The G1 runs at a 500 Hz timestep (0.002 s). mj_forward advances nothing.

q: In a kinematic script, dragging the viewer's Control sliders does nothing. Why?
choices: The sliders write ctrl, which only acts through mj_step
The viewer drops key and mouse input in kinematic mode
ctrl is in degrees while qpos is in radians
mj_forward resets ctrl to zero on every call
why: In a kinematic script ctrl does nothing; the sliders look dead until wired onto qpos by hand.

q: nsite = 4 on the G1. What are the four sites?
choices: Two feet and two IMUs
Two feet and two hands
Four IMUs, two per side
Two hands and two IMUs
why: Feet (left_foot, right_foot) and IMUs (imu_in_torso, imu_in_pelvis). There are no hand sites.

q: How do you read the left hand's position on the G1?
choices: data.xpos of the left_wrist_yaw_link body
data.site_xpos of the left_hand site
The torso IMU site plus the arm length
data.xpos of the left_elbow_link body
why: nsite = 4 has no hand sites, so a hand is read from xpos of the wrist-yaw body (the arm's leaf).

q: How symmetric is the G1 model, left to right?
choices: To 10 µm: shoulder y +0.100220 vs −0.100210
To machine precision: about 10⁻¹⁶ m everywhere
To 1 mm: the CAD meshes were rounded on export
To 10 µm: the two hips differ by that much
why: The only asymmetric body_pos is the shoulder pitch link. A CAD artefact in the model, not a bug in your code.

q: Left shoulder at y = +0.100220 m, right at y = −0.100210 m. How far is the right one from the exact mirror image of the left?
choices: 10 µm
1 µm
100 µm
0.1 µm
why: Mirror of the left is −0.100220; the difference from −0.100210 is 0.000010 m = 10 µm, one part in ten thousand.

q: Mirrored hand positions agree only to about 10⁻⁵ m, not 10⁻¹⁶. Diagnosis?
choices: A 10 µm asymmetry in the MJCF itself, not a bug
A bug in mirror(): pitch must be negated as well
Floating-point round-off growing along the arm
A quaternion read scalar-last somewhere in the arm
why: The shoulder body_pos values differ by 10 µm. Do not 'fix' the mirror code chasing it, and never assert 1e-16 near it.

q: set_pose bends both legs into a squat and the feet end 0.111 m off the floor. Diagnosis?
choices: Correct: set_pose pins the pelvis, so bent legs are shorter
A bug: set_pose forgot to call mj_forward afterwards
A bug: the squat angles were applied in degrees
Correct only because the servos were switched off
why: Kinematics places a pose; it does not settle a robot. A real squat lowers the pelvis by about that amount, which IK and the walker decide.

q: What does soc4180.set_pose do besides writing your angles?
choices: Resets to stand first (unless reset=None), then calls mj_forward
Steps physics until the robot settles onto the floor
Lowers the pelvis so the feet stay on the floor
Copies the angles into ctrl for the servos to track
why: Each pose is then a complete description, not something accumulated from earlier calls, and the x quantities are ready when it returns. It never lowers the pelvis.

q: With the pelvis pinned by set_pose, how far does a symmetric squat lift the feet?
why: 0.111 m for the 2b squat (hip −0.6, knee 1.2, ankle −0.6). 0.037 m is week 2's single-leg crouch; 0.035 m is the foot site's height above the spheres.

q: Why write set_pose(model, data, left_elbow=1.2) rather than data.qpos[25] = 1.2?
choices: Ids move when the MJCF changes, names do not; wrong slots never raise
qpos[25] raises an IndexError on the G1, whose arm starts at 26
Indexing qpos by slot is far slower than a name lookup
qpos[25] is read in degrees, while set_pose takes radians
why: Write names, not slots. qpos[25] is the left elbow today, but the one bug you cannot catch by reading is a valid index that means the wrong joint.

q: You want to measure how the torso moves. Which point should you track?
choices: The imu_in_torso site, not the torso_link origin
The torso_link body origin, the centre of the torso
The pelvis IMU, which sees everything mounted above it
The head, which is welded rigidly to the torso
why: torso_link's origin lies on the waist axes and barely moves (0.4 mm under waist_yaw, 0 under roll and pitch); the IMU site moves 4/15/15 mm.
